description: We are two brothers who love technology, space, and building things that solve real problems. Developers and cybersecurity consultants. We build web apps, automation tools, and AI-powered solutions. We also work in OSINT and data analysis, so we're comfortable turning messy data into clear insights.
summary: In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by "blinking" two photos of the same patch of sky until something moved. SPHEREx Blink brings that technique to NASA's newest all-sky infrared survey. Type a star name or coordinates, and the app downloads real SPHEREx cutouts from NASA's IRSA archive, corrects each star's proper motion using Gaia DR3, aligns and stacks the images by observation epoch, and plays them as a live animation. Moving or changing objects then jump out to the eye. It also shows a real 102-band spectrum for each pixel, a light curve, and 2MASS context. All five required targets load instantly, plus three southern-sky targets chosen for viewers in Colombia and Latin America. The app is bilingual (EN/ES), mobile-first and works on low bandwidth, so anyone can practice the same method used to hunt for an unseen planet in infrared all-sky data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx Blink turns the NASA SPHEREx all-sky infrared archive into a live "blink comparator", the method Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto in 1930 and that the Backyard Worlds citizen-science project still uses today. The user enters a star name or coordinates, and the app shows how that patch of sky changes between SPHEREx observation epochs, so motion or variability is easy to see. Other views: a real spectrum for each pixel (102 bands), a light curve, a 2MASS sky view served by NASA/IRSA, a difference mode, a deep stack and an RGB composite.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Proper-motion correction: Gaia DR3 astrometry is propagated to the epoch of each SPHEREx observation. Without this, a fast star like Barnard's Star (10.4"/year, about 269" since J2000) would leave the frame.

2. Real cutouts: SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images (DR1 + QR3) are cut out on the server through IRSA's SIA2 service.

3. Alignment and stacking: images are grouped by epoch and combined with a variance-weighted mean. Bad pixels are masked, and images are reprojected to SPHEREx's native 6.2"/pixel scale.

4. Playback: the epochs are animated so changes stand out.

WHY IT IS SCIENTIFICALLY VALID

We show the data as it is. Saturated cores are marked in white with a red border, not hidden. Masked pixels appear in grey. Images use an asinh stretch clipped at the 1-99.5 percentiles. A "J2000" marker shows how far the star has moved since 2000. Pixels are drawn as real 6.2" squares, because SPHEREx trades sharpness for 102-color all-sky coverage. For brown dwarfs that Gaia cannot see, we use proper motions from published studies. No image or scientific data in the app was generated by AI.

HOW WE ADDRESSED THE CHALLENGE (PLANET X)

A distant planet like the proposed Planet Nine would be cold, so it would shine mainly in the infrared. It would also be faint and move slowly against the background stars. The classic way to find such an object is to compare images of the same sky taken at different times and look for what moves: the blink technique. SPHEREx Blink applies it to SPHEREx, which maps the whole sky more than once. We tested the pipeline on the five required targets: Barnard's Star (very fast proper motion), Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb and WISE 0855-0714 (cold, faint brown dwarfs, the closest analogues to a cold planet), and RW Aurigae and R Draconis (variable objects, to tell real motion apart from brightness changes). We added three southern-sky targets visible from Colombia: Proxima Centauri, Luhman 16 AB and UGPS 0722-05.

IMPACT FOR CITIZEN SCIENCE

The app is bilingual (Spanish/English), mobile-first and has a low-bandwidth mode, so it works on everyday phones and connections. A built-in tutorial ("how to detect a moving object") teaches the method step by step. Shareable URLs and an embed button make it easy to use in classrooms and outreach. Accessibility checks with axe-core report 0 violations.

TOOLS

Web front end deployed on Vercel, Python backend, Aladin Lite (CDS), and the IRSA SIA2 and HiPS services. Code: https://github.com/Rikethken93/spherex-blink

USE OF AI

The code was written with Claude Code (Anthropic) under our team's direction. The concept, the target list, the requirements and all design decisions are our own, and every data-access decision was checked against the real archives (see DECISIONS.md in the repository). No AI was used to generate images or scientific data: every sky image in the app and in our demo video is real SPHEREx data. The voice-over and background music in our demo video were generated by software (Kokoro text-to-speech), as noted in the video metadata.
